<reason>Side A (CON) controlled the decisive clash from Rebuttal 1 onward: the twin questions of what sanction enforces a binding quota and what mechanism retains relocated applicants. Side B answered the pressure honestly but conceded both points — the sanction is financial and there is no retention mechanism — which let A frame the entire proposition as converging on A's own flexible-solidarity endpoint "with a court summons attached." A also landed a clean catch on B's claim that the relocated man "never lands on Lesbos," since relocation follows landing and registration. B's best counter — that the real difference is where the obligation sits by default, charity versus system, and that frontline states themselves demand redistribution — was genuinely strong and never fully dissolved; A's "a state under strain asks for everything" reply was the weakest moment in an otherwise sharp case. B's closing "It is a receipt" was memorable, but A's crystallization ("the same relief, purchased twice: once in cash, once in cohesion") gave the cleaner voting story. A's two clipped turns are minor execution costs. Clear but competitive win for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2, where B's concessions (financial sanction, no retention mechanism) were welded into a single ledger: PRO's "binding quota" cashes out as a fine that funds frontline capacity — i.e., CON's mechanism — after years of litigation and political backlash. B's honest A2 admission ("I cannot promise the man stays in Latvia") plus the caught "never lands on Lesbos" error made this exchange the turning point.</best_rebuttal>
